Share A A A This year’s Melbourne International Film Festival has kicked off. Here we take a closer look at some of what’s on offer. See all stories . With more than 300 films on this year’s program, it’s easy to feel overwhelmed by what’s on offer at Melbourne’s annual cinematic banquet. Our reviewers have done some of the heavy lifting, watching features, animations and documentaries from home and abroad. Among their list of recommendations is the film that was favoured to win at Cannes … The Dreamed Adventure Photo: MIFF Veska is an archaeologist, returned to the remote country where she grew up to dig into Bulgaria’s history, but her sharp dealings with local gangsters suggest that her own buried past is murkier than she might want to admit. German filmmaker Valeska Grisebach (whose previous film, Western , was also set in Bulgaria) enjoys pulling at the threads of male-coded genres; Veska, portrayed by amateur actor Yana Radeva, has something of Clint Eastwood about her, in a narrative that is signposted as a crime thriller. Those crimes remain largely unexplained, however; what counts here are the characters, their drinking banter, ambiguous alliances and the wildness of this country, which feels like the far edge of the world. SB We Are The Shaggs Photo: MIFF Everyone in Ken Kwapis’ documentary has a hot take on The Shaggs, the outsider-art pop group formed by three teenage sisters in Fremont, New Hampshire, in 1969 under the supervision of their tyrannical father. Gradually a cult formed around them, despite their total lack of conventional musical skill. But how far was this simply ironic appreciation, and how far were fans drawn to their unique musical world? A Hollywood veteran well known for his work on sitcoms such as The Offic e, Kwapis might seem like a surprising figure to be telling this story. But the film gains from his light, sympathetic touch, as well as his willingness to keep an open mind on the question of what makes art good or bad. JW Advertisement Elephants in the Fog Photo: MIFF Related Article Australian film Writer, director and actor times two: Harvey Zielinski’s debut double act In a small Nepalese village, a household of kinnar – transgender women traditionally supposed to bring good fortune to weddings and births – use their spiritual gifts to help local farmers keep wild elephants at bay. Director Abinash Bikram Shah provides an insight into the kinnars’ cult, now widely threatened with suppression, within what is loosely a detective story. Kinnar matriarch Pirati (the engaging real-life trans activist Pushpa Thing Lama) is about to formally adopt her favourite trans daughter when the young woman disappears. Pirati suspects murder, but the police are not interested in these outsiders; she must run the culprit to ground. Exotic and inspiring, this is also a dark look at a very specific misogyny. SB The Fence Photo: MIFF Set on a construction site in West Africa, Claire Denis’ adaptation of a play by the late French writer Bernard-Marie Koltes remains wilfully theatrical, yet depends on making us feel the unglamorous starkness of the desert setting, where there’s little to distract from the core realities of work, desire and death. The symbolic fence of the title separates the site’s American foreman, Horn (Matt Dillon) from a visitor (Isaach de Bankole) who comes to claim the body of a dead worker. Much of the film is built on the contrast between Dillon’s mannered gestures and de Bankole’s stillness, but Mia McKenna-Bruce ( How To Have Sex ) is more intriguing than either as Horn’s younger wife, the least predictable element in the design. JW Advertisement Fatherland Photo: MIFF Pipped at the post for the Cannes Palme D’Or, Pawel Pawlikowski’s diamond-sharp sliver of history was nevertheless the festival’s winner for me. Nobel Prize-winning German author Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler, oozing exhaustion with life) tours the two Germanys in the aftermath of World War II, accompanied by his stolidly self-sufficient daughter Erika (Sandra Huller), to give lectures on the 200th anniversary of Goethe’s death. Both sides of the internal border want to claim Goethe and Mann as their own, despite Mann’s insistence on a tolerant, liberal European humanism that no longer pleases the powerful. Pawlikowski ( Ida, Cold War ) focuses on the Manns’ intimate exchanges, but always with an eye for details that conjure their crucial cultural context. SB Blue Heron Photo: MIFF The Hungarian immigrant family in this first feature by Canadian director Sophy Romvari is unhappy in a way uniquely its own. The life of each family member revolves around the troubled oldest son, Jeremy (Edik Beddoes), who spends much of his time alone in his room drawing maps, and when he does go outside is regularly in trouble with the police. This is an innately painful subject, especially as Romvari has confirmed the story is based loosely on memories of her own childhood. But the tone is equal parts sad, tranquil and perplexing: the tricky structure moves between the 1990s and the present, underlining that reality isn’t identical with our vision of it, either in the moment or long after. JW Rose Advertisement Photo: MIFF Related Article Australian film Writer, director and actor times two: Harvey Zielinski’s debut double act Sandra Huller shows once again what a great screen actor she is in this austere historic fable, set after the Thirty Years War in an anonymous German village. Nobody there recognises the soldier who comes back to claim his father’s old farm, but he is soon accepted as the community sees how hard he works. He has a secret, however, which isn’t rumbled because it is so unthinkable: the village’s new success story is a woman. Austrian director Markus Schleinzer, shooting within a narrow palette of greys, maintains a constant tension as Rose’s inevitable unmasking looms ever closer; while his style certainly isn’t naturalistic, the story – for which there are many real-life precedents – has the ring of truth. SB Chronovisor Photo: MIFF Shot on 16-milimetre film by the US team of Kevin Walker and Jack Auen, this eccentric micro-budget fantasy combines elements of conspiracy thriller, gallery installation, and homage to the written word (Jorge Luis Borges and Roberto Bolano are among the writers name-checked in the credits). At the centre of it all is the (loosely) real-life story of a Benedictine monk who claimed in the 1970s to have invented a machine that could photograph the past, inspiring the wild-goose chase which the academic heroine (Anne Laure Sellier) undertakes decades on. Literally speaking, almost nothing happens on screen, yet the intangible nature of the whole story still inspires fascination and even dread. JW Advertisement Hen Photo: MIFF Eight real hens play one plucky, clucky fictional fowl whose adventures provide a bird’s-eye view of human wickedness: an oddity, certainly, but a thoroughly good egg. Hungarian surrealist Gyorgy Palfi is remembered fondly for the fabulously grotesque Taxidermist ; this film, constrained by the limits of avian actors, is more conventional and thoroughly heartwarming. Hen ’s heroine escapes the battery farm where she was laid, has a couple of scrapes where she is almost eaten, then fetches up as the favoured pet of an old man whose disreputable son-in-law is using his former diner as a holding station for his people-smuggling business. Palfi’s persuasive genius is to tell this story without CGI tricks and without anthropomorphising the star: from beak to tail feathers, she’s always just a bird. SB MIFF runs August 6-23, miff.com.au

Beállítom Elérte Omán tengerpartját a júniusban egy orosz hajóból kiömlő olajfolt – írja a Reuters . A folt néhány nap alatt 400 négyzetkilométeresről 2000 négyzetkilométeresre nőtt, és egy 40 kilométeres partszakaszt érinthet – többek között egy olyan szigetét, ami több állatfaj, köztük bálnák otthonaként környezetvédelmi területnek számít. Ha nem kezelik, a legnagyobb ilyen katasztrófává válhat az elmúlt évekből. A Caroline Bezengi nevű hajó csaknem egymillió hordó orosz kőolajat szállított, és Ázsiába tartott. Először június 8-án, Jemen partjainál jeleztek problémát a hajóról. A Reuters több forrása szerint az eddigi vizsgálatok arra utaltak, hogy robbanás történt a fedélzeten, a hajó elleni támadásért azonban egyelőre senki sem vállalta a felelősséget. A környező háború és szankciók megnehezítik az olajfolt eltisztítását. A nemzetközi olajkiömlésekkel foglalkozó IOPC közölte, hogy nem foglalkoznak az üggyel, mert háborús cselekmény lehet a hátterében, és nem egy egyszerű balesetről van szó. Hajókövetési adatok szerint a Caroline Bezengi áprilisban Oroszország fekete-tengeri Novorosszijszk kikötőjében vette fel rakományát, majd május végén áthaladt a Szuezi-csatornán. A 2001-ben épített hajó az orosz árnyékflottához tartozó régebbi olajszállító tankerek egyike. Ezek a hajók nem rendelkeznek nyugati biztosítási fedezettel, és különböző országok zászlaja alatt közlekednek, hogy elrejtsék tényleges tulajdonosi hátterüket. A hajóval szemben az Európai Unió, Ukrajna, az Egyesült Királyság, Kanada és Svájc által bevezetett szankciók vannak érvényben. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! https://www.dw.com/en/saxony-anhalt-smal.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5JIs8 Saxony-Anhalt is governed from the state parliament in Magdeburg Image: ArTo/Zoonar/IMAGO Advertisement It's rare that a state parliament election in Germany attracts as much media interest as this one in Saxony-Anhalt . On September 6, 2026, the 1.7 million eligible voters in the eastern German state will decide whether the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party can form a state government for the first time. So far, there has not been a head of government who belonged to a proven far-right party in post- World War II Germany — at neither federal nor state level. That would change if AfD lead candidate Ulrich Siegmund were to be elected to this position, since the Office for the Protection of the Constitution in Saxony Anhalt already classified the AfD as such in 2023. Siegmund's chances of a historical triumph are high: For months the AfD has been comfortably leading the polls with well over 40% of the vote. AfD, CDU and Left Party will get into parliament Aside from the AfD, there are only two other parties who can count on being included in the next state parliament: The conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of current State Premier Sven Schulze and the socialist Left Party , which is traditionally strong in eastern Germany, the former socialist GDR . All other parties have cause for concern they could fail to reach the 5% threshold of votes necessary for entry into parliaments in Germany. This even applies to the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), who currently form part of the federal government coalition with the CDU and its Bavarian counterpart, the Christian Social Union (CSU). SPD, Greens, FDP, BSW might not make the 5% mark The SPD is losing popularity nationwide . In Saxony-Anhalt, they are polling below the 8% they won five years ago. The third party in Saxony-Anhalt's current governing coalition, formed in 2021, has even fewer hopes: The neoliberal Free Democrats (FDP) are polling only about 3%. Following the FDP's failure in the Bundestag general election of 2025 and multiple defeats at the state level, supporters are bracing themselves for the next setback. The environmentalist Greens are also concerned about returning to the state parliament. The party, whose core voter base is in wealthy western German cities, is vehemently rejected by many voters in rural areas because of its climate policies and multicultural vision of society. Concern over Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) And then there is the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW), founded in 2024 by its namesake, a former Left Party co-leader. The party is economically left-leaning, but socially right-wing conservative and populist. This is its first time participating in a state election in Saxony-Anhalt. After the BSW gained 6.2% of the vote in the European parliament elections in 2024 and won results of between about 12% and 16% in the eastern German states of Brandenburg, Saxony and Thuringia during its first year, it failed by only a few thousand votes to reach the 5% hurdle to enter German parliament in the 2025 general election. The BSW never really recovered from this setback. They went on to be defeated in three further state parliament elections. The party also has cause for concern in Saxony-Anhalt, where it has been polling under 5%. Should it win representation after all, Sahra Wagenknecht has already announced that her party's lawmakers would not vote an AfD premier into office, but abstain from the vote paving the way for him to win a majority in parliament and take office. Considering the poor polling numbers for the BSW in Saxony-Anhalt, political scientist Oliver Lembcke speaks of an "endgame" for the party as a whole. What if Germany's far-right AfD party wins in Saxony-Anhalt? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Small parties could prevent absolute majority for the AfD The fact is: The more parties fail to reach the threshold, the higher the likelihood of the Alternative for Germany will be able to govern alone. On the other hand, if aside from the AfD, the CDU, Left Party and SPD win representation in the next Saxony-Anhalt parliament, and those three parties together hold more seats than the AfD, the situation is complicated. This is because in 2018 the CDU adopted a so-called " resolution of incompatibility ," which rejects cooperation with both the AfD and the Left Party. If the CDU sticks to this, forming even a minority government would be very difficult, perhaps impossible. Could the CDU form a minority government? Political scientist Lembcke from Ruhr University Bochum in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia argues that the CDU should have adapted its incompatibility resolution to the changed conditions of the party systems and political landscape. Because it has failed to do so, this issue could now escalate drastically in Saxony-Anhalt. The Left Party is prepared to support Premier Sven Schulze of the CDU to secure a second term. "In recent years, we, the Left Party, have shown that we take responsibility for this country. Especially when it comes to inhibiting the AfD," Left Party co-leader Luigi Pantisano told television broadcaster ZDF. He pointed to the states of Thuringia and Saxony , where the CDU leads coalition governments without a parliamentary majority and depends on the support of the Left Party. Given the foreseeably complicated situation, one thing is clear ahead of the September 6 election: either Saxony-Anhalt faces an incredibly difficult coalition-building process, or the state will be governed by the AfD — if the party profits from the failure of many small parties and thereby receives an absolute majority in the state parliament. https://www.dw.com/en/france-sabotage-su.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MUIX The network operator said traffic on the line has been halted [FILE: June 2026] Image: Syspeo/SIPA/picture alliance Advertisement A train derailed on Friday evening between the cities of Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France , authorities said, with local media citing police as saying sabotage may have been at play in the incident. At least 44 people were injured in the accident, which occurred near the municipalities of Cleon and Tourville-la-Riviere at around 7:30 p.m. local time (18:30 UTC), the Seine-Maritime prefect said in a statement . One of ​the injured, a young woman, was in a critical state and was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen, the local authority added. The train was carrying around 180 passengers when it derailed, national rail company SNCF and the prefect said. What else do we know about the train derailment? French Transport Minister Tabarot said 140 firefighters were at the scene. Local authorities have urged the public to avoid the area. The French rail network operator SNCF Reseau said traffic on the line had been suspended. "The priority is to care for the passengers and then to restore safe operating conditions," SNCF Reseau said. ​A police spokesperson said the train derailed after hitting an unidentified object. A piece of rail that might have been involved has been found on the track, according to police reports. Illustration: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty Images/Tika Basnet View image in fullscreen ‘These profiles were … listing specific interests in an attempt to appeal to … individuals in law enforcement,’ the FBI memo said. Illustration: Rita Liu/The Guardian/Getty Images/Tika Basnet FBI FBI warned ICE agents could be targeted by fake ‘tradwife’ dating profiles, memo reveals Exclusive: Internal FBI memo, reviewed by the Guardian, said women wanted to dox and ‘embarrass’ agents, but provided few details Sam Levin in Los Angeles Thu 17 Sep 2026 10.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 10.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The FBI internally warned that a group of women were creating fake online dating accounts with “tradwife” aesthetics in an effort to lure US immigration agents and “dox” them. The FBI in Chicago disseminated a brief memo to other law enforcement officials across the US on the potential threat to agents in February, warning that “as of late January 2026, a small group of women allegedly were creating fictitious online dating profiles with the purpose of attracting and then doxxing law enforcement participating in immigration enforcement”. The report, which was shared with the Guardian, provided few details about the alleged scheme and did not explain the source of the information. “These profiles were incorporating imagery of a ‘traditional wife’ aesthetic and listing specific interests in an attempt to appeal to … individuals in law enforcement,” the FBI continued. “The objective was to lure affiliated law enforcement personnel into an online or in-person interaction under the guise of a date, after which the individuals would be publicly exposed and doxed online. The tactic is intended to generate public embarrassment and deter immigration enforcement activity.” Property of the People , a government-transparency non-profit, obtained the document through a public records request, one of many internal records the group has collected revealing internal law enforcement concerns about activists organizing against Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The FBI’s “situational information report” did not list the dating sites allegedly used by the women or where they were located, nor did it specify whether agents had actually been exposed. The memo aimed “to raise awareness” about this doxing “technique”, the FBI wrote, adding a disclaimer that the report was “not finally evaluated intelligence”. The FBI’s “tradwife” comments were a reference to the trend popularized in recent years by influencers promoting traditional gender roles , with women romanticizing domesticity . “Doxing” generally refers to publishing someone’s private information online without their consent, though the administration has used the term loosely, claiming doxing includes posting videos of officers. The FBI declined to answer detailed questions about the memo, saying the bureau doesn’t generally comment on intelligence briefings. A spokesperson added in an email: “The FBI regularly shares information with our law enforcement partners to assist in protecting the communities they serve as well as protecting those who serve and protect communities. The FBI is committed to ensuring that law enforcement officers are safe from threats or violence while performing their duties.” The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) did not respond to requests for comment. The memo was sent weeks after the New York Post, a conservative outlet, ran a story saying that “lefty TikTokkers” were “orchestrating groups of women” to “chase dick picks and selfies of ICE agents in a twisted scheme to dox them”. That story cited Libs of TikTok, a rightwing account that had posted a screenshot of someone claiming to be part of a Facebook group dedicated to going on dates with agents to expose them. The article listed a handful of posts and videos from users discussing this tactic, though it did not include interviews with anyone who claimed to be duping agents and there was no evidence agents had been tricked. The news coverage did not mention women using “tradwife” imagery, so it’s unclear whether the FBI may have received direct accounts from targeted agents or was simply summarizing social media trends. “It’s absurd the FBI issued a thinly-sourced security alert about ICE agents’ online dating troubles,” Ryan Shapiro, executive director of Property of the People, said in a statement. “It’s equally ludicrous the FBI is spending taxpayer dollars to protect ICE agents from possible ‘embarrassment’ at the hands of a supposed ‘small group of women’ who might name and ridicule them online.” Mike German, a former FBI agent and longtime civil liberties advocate , reviewed the document for the Guardian and said it was odd the briefing did not have footnotes or citations. The briefing said the intelligence came from a “collaborative source”. “The rightwing echo chamber creates threats and the government’s intelligence apparatus just repeats those threats without any context, more detail or any instruction of how agents or officers should respond,” said German, arguing it seemed likely the briefing was inspired by the New York Post story. “They must have run out of other threats.” The document, German added, “reinforces the paranoid ‘us versus them’ mentality within law enforcement”. The briefing comes as US law enforcement has raised increasing alarms about officials, and ICE agents in particular, being “doxed”. More than a dozen internal law enforcement reports, obtained via records requests by Property of the People, include similar warnings about doxing. An October 2025 report from the US army said there was “credible intelligence” that “cartels” had offered to pay gang members and others in the US to dox, assault or kidnap immigration officers. That report cited charges against a man accused of a murder-for-hire plot targeting a top border patrol leader, but the man was found not guilty months later. In a November 2025 report, the FBI warned that AI, facial-recognition and automated data-scraping tools had “increased the scale and accuracy of doxxing attacks” targeting ICE officers. The alert said people had published ICE officers’ names, photos, license plates, locations and family details, citing various crowdsourced efforts by activists to report ICE sightings. In a January 2026 New York police department “terrorism brief”, the NYPD warned of “violent rhetoric” and “extremist messaging” on social media after the killing of Renee Good, including “calls to ‘hunt down’, ‘dox’, and kill ICE personnel”. The report cited a small number of online posts that appeared to call for violence. And a May 2026 alert from Customs and Border Protection (CBP), a branch of DHS, warned that smart glasses, which have cameras, could be used to surveil, record and potentially dox CBP personnel. A CBP spokesperson did not comment directly on the document, but said in an email that smart glasses “pose unique security and intelligence risks because of their ability to discreetly capture audio and video” and the agency continues to monitor technology trends. Property of the People shared records with the Guardian earlier this month showing law enforcement across the US have grown increasingly concerned that smart glasses could be used against officers. Other law enforcement agencies that have raised concerns about ICE agents being doxed in internal records include the FBI in Los Angeles, the Amtrak police department, an Idaho law enforcement consortium, a Florida fusion center of local and federal agencies, and the Federal Protective Service, which is also part of DHS. There can be safety concerns if agents’ home addresses or family information is exposed, and two activists were convicted of “stalking” in California after prosecutors said they followed an agent home and publicly disclosed the location. But German argued law enforcement’s claims about doxing were misguided, noting that ICE officers are domestic servants, not “secret agents” whose identities must be shielded: “These are agents working on the public dime. The public has a right to know who they are and what their qualifications and training are.” Explore more on these topics FBI ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) US politics US immigration news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness
